error_modes.label: Mission planning and route briefing conducted as a crew task

texts.0: SP, due to a threat that was present in the minimum threat set but not identified in the brief, planned the VFR navigation route as an individual task and briefed no division of duties between front and rear cockpit. SP covered neither the checkpoint sequence, nor the leg timing responsibility, nor the airspace and terrain constraints along the track. The IP had to stop the briefing and rebuild the route plan with SP before the sortie could be authorized.
texts.1: SP, due to mission planning that did not address the forecast weather at the recovery time, briefed the route without stating who would hold the chart, who would run the clock and who would fly. SP added the missing crew coordination content only after the IP had raised the point verbally more than once, and the plan was completed after the briefing had formally ended. No IP intervention was required in flight.
texts.2: SP, due to a first pass through the route flown without reference to the airspace boundaries along track, briefed the opening legs without assigning lookout and chart-reading responsibility. SP recognized the omission before the briefing ended, restated the division of duties for the whole route and flew the sortie as restated. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP planned the VFR navigation route as a crew task and briefed it accurately and without delay, with checkpoint sequence, timing responsibility, lookout duties and airspace constraints agreed before flight. SP identified the threats along the track in the brief and stated how each would be managed. The sortie was flown as briefed and no IP addition to the plan was required.
texts.4: SP planned every leg of the route as a crew task, including the contingencies for weather, unexpected traffic and checkpoint acquisition failure, and assigned duties for each of them. The brief was complete and unambiguous, the threats along track were identified and paired with a stated countermeasure, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in planning and briefing the route as a crew task, but the crew coordination content was concentrated in the first legs and thinned out toward the turning point and the recovery. The trend across the brief was toward assuming the division of duties rather than stating it. SP is expected to brief duties, timing responsibility and threats for every leg of the route on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP asking who would hold the chart, who would run the clock and who would fly, SP followed the crew task and stated the division of duties after the question on two of the legs. Briefing the route as a crew task without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to state one duty unprompted before doing so for the whole brief.
texts_at.1: SP planned and briefed the route as a crew task inside the standard required at this stage, crew coordination content added only after the IP had raised the point verbally more than once. The trend traces to mission planning addressing the route itself without also addressing the forecast weather at the recovery time. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to address the recovery-time weather during planning itself so crew coordination content is not added afterward.
texts_at.2: SP planned and briefed the route as a crew task inside the standard required at this stage, lookout and chart-reading responsibility not assigned for the opening legs because the first pass through the route did not reference the airspace boundaries along track. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reference the airspace boundaries on the first pass so responsibilities are assigned for the opening legs too.
texts_at.3: SP planned the VFR navigation route as a crew task and briefed it accurately and without delay, checkpoint sequence, timing responsibility, lookout duties and airspace constraints agreed before flight, the small margin tracing to one threat being paired with its countermeasure a beat after the rest of the brief. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to pair every threat with its countermeasure at the same point in the brief so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP planned and briefed the route as a crew task, one duty stated after a verbal question from the IP and the rest stated unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission before the briefing ended, restated the division of duties for the whole route and flew the sortie as restated, without prompting or intervention, after the opening legs had been briefed without assigned lookout and chart-reading responsibility. Referencing the airspace boundaries on the first pass through the route, rather than recognizing the omission before the brief ends, would remove even that restatement. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good crew briefing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP planned the VFR navigation route as a crew task and briefed it accurately and without delay, with checkpoint sequence, timing responsibility, lookout duties and airspace constraints agreed before flight, the threats along the track identified in the brief and paired with a stated countermeasure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good crew briefing discipline.
texts_above.4: SP planned every leg of the route as a crew task, including the contingencies for weather, unexpected traffic and checkpoint acquisition failure, assigning duties for each of them with the brief complete and unambiguous. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent crew briefing discipline.

error_modes.label: Use of the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items

texts.0: SP, due to unfamiliarity with the publication, did not use the IFG/CRM matrix chart at any point of the navigation sortie and could not locate the items applicable to the profile. No matrix item was highlighted in the briefing and none was carried into the debriefing. The IP had to open the chart and work the applicable items with SP before the grade sheet could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete preparation during mission planning, opened the IFG/CRM matrix chart but highlighted items unrelated to the VFR navigation profile flown. SP selected the correct items only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and their discussion was pushed to the end of the debriefing. No action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed review of the chart before the brief, first highlighted a general matrix item instead of the one matching the navigation task actually flown. SP recognized the mismatch without prompting, returned to the IFG/CRM matrix chart and selected the correct items in time for the discussion. No IP direction was needed.
texts.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart accurately and without delay to highlight the CRM items applicable to the navigation sortie. The items selected matched the route flown and the areas covered in the debriefing, and were presented in the standard sequence.
texts.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items and tied each one to a specific event of the route, from planning through the turning point to the recovery. The selection was complete, correct and required no revision by the IP, with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart and met the standard, but selected the minimum number of items and needed a second look at the chart to confirm two of them. The trend was toward picking the familiar items rather than those matching the navigation profile actually flown. SP is expected to preselect the applicable matrix items during mission planning on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP opening the IFG/CRM matrix chart and naming the applicable items, SP followed the selection read back and needed the items named before the grade sheet could be completed. Locating and highlighting an applicable matrix item without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to highlight one item unprompted before doing so for the whole chart.
texts_at.1: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart inside the standard required at this stage, the correct items selected only after repeated verbal direction from the IP. The trend traces to the chart being opened without preparation during mission planning rather than reviewed in advance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the matrix chart during mission planning so the correct items are selected without direction.
texts_at.2: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart inside the standard required at this stage, a general matrix item initially highlighted instead of the one matching the navigation task actually flown, because the chart was reviewed in a rush before the brief. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to review the chart without rushing so the first item highlighted already matches the task flown.
texts_at.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart accurately and without delay to highlight the CRM items applicable to the navigation sortie, items selected matching the route flown and presented in the standard sequence, the small margin tracing to one item being tied to its event a beat after the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to tie every item to its event at the same pace so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart for the sortie, one item highlighted after a verbal call from the IP and the rest highlighted unprompted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the mismatch without prompting, returned to the IFG/CRM matrix chart and selected the correct items in time for the discussion, with no IP direction needed, after a rushed review had first highlighted a general item instead of the one matching the flight. Reviewing the chart without rushing before the brief, rather than recognizing the mismatch afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound IFG/CRM matrix usage.
texts_above.3: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart accurately and without delay to highlight the CRM items applicable to the navigation sortie, the items selected matching the route flown and the areas covered in the debriefing, presented in the standard sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed IFG/CRM matrix usage.
texts_above.4: SP used the IFG/CRM matrix chart to highlight the applicable items and tied each one to a specific event of the route, from planning through the turning point to the recovery, the selection complete and correct. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional IFG/CRM matrix usage.

error_modes.label: Crew communication and information sharing along the navigation legs

texts.0: SP, due to lack of communication of the recognized problem to the other cockpit, did not share an unresolved position doubt and passed no checkpoint, timing or heading information for the whole leg. The IP had no means of knowing what SP believed the aircraft position to be until the track error had already taken the aircraft off the planned route. The IP had to take control of the navigation and reestablish the aircraft on track before the sortie could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of the navigation state, passed checkpoint and timing calls that did not say whether the checkpoint had actually been identified. SP stated the position, the time and the heading correction clearly only after the IP had asked for them more than once, and the information arrived after the leg it referred to had been flown. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a high radio workload in the first part of the leg, omitted the checkpoint and timing call at the initial point and left the other cockpit without a shared picture of the navigation state. SP recognized the omission without prompting, passed a complete position, time and fuel update and maintained the agreed calls for the rest of the route. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP passed accurate and timely checkpoint, timing, heading and fuel information at each briefed point, so that both cockpits held the same picture of the navigation state throughout the route. Doubts about checkpoint identification were stated as doubts rather than left implicit, and radio and intercom transmissions did not compete with each other.
texts.4: SP kept the navigation state shared with the other cockpit continuously, stating the position, the confidence in it and the intended correction before being asked. Communication was structured, plain and separated from the radio calls in workload, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on sharing the navigation state, but the calls became shorter and less complete as the workload increased toward the turning point. The trend was toward passing the heading and omitting the fuel and timing elements of the update. SP is expected to keep the checkpoint, time and fuel content in every position call on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP asking what SP believed the aircraft position to be at each checkpoint, SP followed with the position, time and heading read back after the question on three of the legs. Sharing checkpoint, timing and heading information with the other cockpit without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to share one position call unprompted before doing so for every leg.
texts_at.1: SP shared checkpoint, timing and heading information with the other cockpit inside the standard required at this stage, position, time and heading correction stated clearly only after the IP had asked for them more than once. The trend traces to checkpoint and timing calls not stating whether the checkpoint had actually been identified. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to state explicitly whether a checkpoint has been identified in every call so the information does not need to be asked for.
texts_at.2: SP shared checkpoint, timing and heading information with the other cockpit inside the standard required at this stage, the checkpoint and timing call at the initial point omitted during high radio workload in the first part of the leg. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to protect the checkpoint and timing call from radio workload so it is not omitted.
texts_at.3: SP passed accurate and timely checkpoint, timing, heading and fuel information at each briefed point so both cockpits held the same picture of the navigation state throughout the route, doubts stated as doubts rather than left implicit, the small margin tracing to one fuel element being added a beat after the rest of the update. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to include the fuel element with the rest of the update every time so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP shared checkpoint, timing and heading information with the other cockpit, one call following a verbal question from the IP and the rest shared unprompted. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission without prompting, passed a complete position, time and fuel update and maintained the agreed calls for the rest of the route, with no IP prompting needed, after the checkpoint and timing call at the initial point had been omitted during high radio workload. Protecting the checkpoint and timing call from radio workload from the start, rather than recognizing the omission afterward, would remove even that gap. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid crew communication discipline.
texts_above.3: SP passed accurate and timely checkpoint, timing, heading and fuel information at each briefed point, so that both cockpits held the same picture of the navigation state throughout the route, doubts about checkpoint identification stated as doubts rather than left implicit. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed crew communication discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept the navigation state shared with the other cockpit continuously, stating the position, the confidence in it and the intended correction before being asked, communication structured, plain and separated from the radio calls in workload. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding crew communication discipline.

error_modes.label: Workload distribution between aircraft control, navigation and lookout

texts.0: SP, due to poor workload distribution that left one crew member doing every job, attempted to fly the aircraft, read the chart, run the timing and transmit at the same time along the whole leg. Aircraft control and lookout were both abandoned while SP worked the chart head-down, and no task was passed to the other cockpit. The IP had to take control of the aircraft to restore the flight path and the lookout.
texts.1: SP, due to failure to shed a secondary task when workload increased, kept the chart work and the radio together during the turn onto the next leg and let the lookout lapse. SP passed the non-essential task to the other cockpit only after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the rebalance came after the turn had been completed. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the chart work inside the turn, began the checkpoint search while still correcting the heading and briefly lost the outside scan. SP recognized the saturation without prompting, deferred the chart work until the aircraft was established on heading and reestablished the lookout. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP distributed the workload so that aircraft control, navigation and lookout were each served at the appropriate point of the leg, with chart work planned for the straight and level segments. Secondary tasks were deferred or passed to the other cockpit as workload rose, and the outside scan was maintained accurately and without interruption.
texts.4: SP anticipated the workload peaks of the route and moved the chart work, the fuel check and the radio calls clear of them before they occurred. Aircraft control and lookout were never displaced by a navigation task, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on workload distribution, but the rebalancing was reactive and came only once the outside scan had already narrowed. The trend was toward completing the chart task in progress rather than deferring it when the workload rose. SP is expected to plan chart and fuel work clear of turns and checkpoint acquisition on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP directing which task to pass to the other cockpit as workload rose, SP followed the direction and needed it given on two occasions during the route. Distributing workload between aircraft control, navigation and lookout without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to pass one task unprompted before doing so as workload requires it.
texts_at.1: SP distributed workload between aircraft control, navigation and lookout inside the standard required at this stage, the non-essential task passed to the other cockpit only after repeated verbal direction from the IP. The trend traces to chart work and radio being kept together during a turn rather than one being shed as workload increased. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to shed one of the two tasks as workload increases so the pass to the other cockpit does not need direction.
texts_at.2: SP distributed workload between aircraft control, navigation and lookout inside the standard required at this stage, the outside scan briefly lost while the checkpoint search was begun during a heading correction. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the heading correction before beginning the checkpoint search so the outside scan is not lost during it.
texts_at.3: SP distributed the workload so that aircraft control, navigation and lookout were each served at the appropriate point of the leg, chart work planned for the straight and level segments, secondary tasks deferred as workload rose, the small margin tracing to one deferral being decided a beat after the workload rose rather than anticipated before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to anticipate every deferral before the workload rises so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP distributed workload between aircraft control, navigation and lookout, one task passed after a verbal direction from the IP and the rest passed unprompted. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the saturation without prompting, deferred the chart work until the aircraft was established on heading and reestablished the lookout, with no IP prompting or intervention needed, after the outside scan had briefly been lost during a checkpoint search begun mid-turn. Completing the heading correction before beginning the checkpoint search, rather than recognizing the saturation during it, would remove even that lapse. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady crew workload distribution.
texts_above.3: SP distributed the workload so that aircraft control, navigation and lookout were each served at the appropriate point of the leg, with chart work planned for the straight and level segments, secondary tasks deferred or passed to the other cockpit as workload rose. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate crew workload distribution.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the workload peaks of the route and moved the chart work, the fuel check and the radio calls clear of them before they occurred, aircraft control and lookout never displaced by a navigation task. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary crew workload distribution.

error_modes.label: Application of the CRM concept when analyzing route deviations and divert decisions

texts.0: SP, due to a briefed decision point that was passed without any decision being made, worked the deteriorating route situation alone and applied no CRM concept to the analysis. SP made no assessment of the remaining fuel, the weather ahead and the available alternates, and used neither the other cockpit nor the agencies available on the radio as a resource. The IP had to stop the navigation problem and direct the divert before the situation could be resolved.
texts.1: SP, due to the absence of explicit divert criteria in the mission brief, analyzed the unplanned route change on the basis of a single factor and did not state the alternatives to the other cockpit. SP considered fuel, weather and alternates together only after the IP had raised each of them verbally, and the decision was taken after the point at which it should have been made. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial focus on regaining the planned track, began the analysis of the weather ahead without stating the fuel available for the diversion. SP recognized the gap without prompting, restated the problem to the other cockpit with fuel, weather and alternates together and reached a decision within the leg. No IP direction was needed.
texts.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when analyzing the route deviation, stating the problem, the fuel and weather constraints and the available options to the other cockpit before deciding. The decision was made at the briefed decision point rather than after it, and the resulting plan was passed to both cockpits and to the controlling agency.
texts.4: SP treated the changed route situation as a crew problem from the first indication, defined the decision point and the criteria that would trigger the divert, and used every resource available inside and outside the cockpit. The analysis was complete, the decision was timely and reversible, and deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in analyzing the route deviation as a crew task, but the options were stated only once the preferred plan had already been chosen. The trend was toward confirming the first solution rather than comparing the alternatives. SP is expected to state the divert criteria and the decision point before the leg on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP raising fuel, weather and the available alternates in turn, SP followed the analysis and needed each factor raised before the divert decision could be reached. Applying the CRM concept to a route deviation without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to state one factor unprompted before analyzing the whole deviation independently.
texts_at.1: SP applied the CRM concept to analyzing route deviations and divert decisions inside the standard required at this stage, fuel, weather and alternates considered together only after the IP had raised each of them verbally. The trend traces to the unplanned route change being analyzed on a single factor rather than the full set from the start. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to consider fuel, weather and alternates together from the first indication of a route change so the full set does not need to be raised individually.
texts_at.2: SP applied the CRM concept to analyzing route deviations and divert decisions inside the standard required at this stage, the fuel available for a diversion not stated while the weather ahead was first analyzed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to state the fuel available at the same moment weather is first analyzed so it is not omitted from that first pass.
texts_at.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when analyzing the route deviation, stating the problem, the fuel and weather constraints and the available options to the other cockpit before deciding, the decision made at the briefed decision point, the small margin tracing to the resulting plan being passed to the controlling agency a beat after both cockpits rather than with them. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to pass the plan to the agency together with both cockpits so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.1: SP applied the CRM concept to the route deviation, one factor stated after a verbal question from the IP and the rest stated unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the gap without prompting, restated the problem to the other cockpit with fuel, weather and alternates together and reached a decision within the leg, with no IP direction needed, after fuel available had not been stated while the weather ahead was first analyzed. Stating fuel available at the same moment weather is first analyzed, rather than recognizing the gap afterward, would remove even that restatement. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable CRM-based divert decision making.
texts_above.3: SP applied the CRM concept to the maximum extent when analyzing the route deviation, stating the problem, the fuel and weather constraints and the available options to the other cockpit before deciding, the decision made at the briefed decision point rather than after it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good CRM-based divert decision making.
texts_above.4: SP treated the changed route situation as a crew problem from the first indication, defined the decision point and the criteria that would trigger the divert, and used every resource available inside and outside the cockpit. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior CRM-based divert decision making.

error_modes.label: Debriefing self-assessment and identification of CRM development areas

texts.0: SP, due to reviewing the sortie only by whether the checkpoints were reached, took no part in the CRM discussion at the debriefing and offered no assessment of the coordination errors made along the route. SP identified no area for CRM development and attributed the track and timing errors entirely to the conditions. The IP had to conduct the CRM debriefing alone and complete the CRM box of the grade sheet without any input from SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a debriefing prepared from memory without reference to the route log, described the navigation events but not the crew coordination behind them. SP identified a CRM development area only after the IP had named the events verbally more than once, and the discussion ran past the point where the remaining items could be covered. No further action beyond the extended debriefing was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reconstruction of the sortie leg by leg rather than by crew action, first omitted the coordination failure at the turning point from the self-assessment. SP recognized the omission without prompting, raised the event, stated its effect on the route timing and proposed a specific improvement for the next sortie. No IP prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP assessed his/her own CRM performance accurately and without delay at the debriefing, identified the specific areas for development and stated where crew coordination had enhanced the navigation task and flight safety. The discussion covered the graded CRM items applicable to the sortie and the CRM box of the grade sheet was completed at the end of the debriefing.
texts.4: SP led the CRM portion of the debriefing, linked each coordination behavior to its effect on the route accuracy, the timing and the flight safety, and proposed measurable improvements for the next navigation sortie. The self-assessment matched the events as observed and required no correction by the IP, with negligible deviation from the expected standard.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard in the CRM self-assessment, but the areas identified were general rather than tied to the specific events of the route. The trend was toward accepting the IP's assessment rather than offering an independent one. SP is expected to bring two self-identified CRM development areas, referenced to specific points of the route, to the next debriefing.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the coordination events of the route at the debriefing, SP followed the discussion and identified a development area after two events were named. Assessing CRM performance at the debriefing without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to identify one development area unprompted before assessing the whole sortie independently.
texts_at.1: SP assessed CRM performance at the debriefing inside the standard required at this stage, a CRM development area identified only after the IP had named the events verbally more than once. The trend traces to the debriefing being prepared from memory rather than from the route log. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prepare the debriefing from the route log so a development area is identified without the events being named first.
texts_at.2: SP assessed CRM performance at the debriefing inside the standard required at this stage, a coordination failure at the turning point initially omitted from the self-assessment because the sortie was reconstructed leg by leg rather than by crew action. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reconstruct the sortie by crew action, not only by leg, so a coordination failure is not omitted.
texts_at.3: SP assessed CRM performance accurately and without delay at the debriefing, identifying specific areas for development and stating where crew coordination had enhanced the navigation task and flight safety, the small margin tracing to one graded item being covered a beat after the rest of the discussion. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to cover every graded item at the same pace as the rest of the discussion so this small margin is removed.

error_modes.label: Exact transfer of A/C control phraseology and coordination of the shared navigation systems between cockpits
error_modes.source: technique:1.15 Transfer of A/C and Systems Control

texts.0: SP, due to using words such as it or jet in lieu of the term A/C, left the pilot flying role undefined at a checkpoint handover and released the controls before the other pilot had positively assumed them. SP did not shake the control stick and reconfigured the GPS and the RMU at the same moment, so both cockpits were making inputs on the A/C and on the same system under the last use, last in control logic. The IP had to state the transfer, take the controls and rebuild the route on the navigation display.
texts.1: SP, due to an abbreviated transfer call that omitted the term A/C, left the pilot flying role ambiguous while the other cockpit was resetting the RMU, and did not shake the control stick when assuming control. SP used the exact words only after the IP had directed it verbally more than once, and one EFIS change was made in the meantime without being communicated. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention on the next checkpoint at the moment of the handover, made the transfer call without noticeably shaking the control stick, leaving the assumption of control unconfirmed for a few seconds. SP recognized this without prompting, repeated I have the A/C with a positive shake of the stick, and stated which cockpit held the GPS before the next leg began. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP used the exact words You have the A/C and I have the A/C at every transfer and shook the control stick noticeably when assuming control, so only one pilot was flying at any point of the route. SP retained control of the canopy, RMU, GPS and EFIS unless a transfer of that system had been clearly communicated, and the other cockpit called the system back when finished. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP applied the transfer phraseology as a fixed habit pattern in both directions, including the transfers directed by the IP during the navigation legs, and never relinquished control until the other pilot had positively assumed it. Systems use was coordinated item by item, so no inadvertent input occurred on the navigation displays, and the intercom failure alternative was briefed and rehearsed. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP met the standard on transfer of A/C and systems control, but the confirming stick shake was weak on two handovers and the term A/C was replaced once by an informal word. The trend was toward relying on the other cockpit to infer both the transfer and the ownership of the GPS rather than stating them. SP is expected to use the exact phraseology with a positive stick shake, and to call the system transfer, on every handover of the next sortie.

The IP had to reject the plan and restructure the profile before the sortie could proceed.

texts.2: SP, due to the attention given to the route calculations, initially assessed only the environmental conditions and omitted the mission profile factors. SP recognized the gap during the same briefing without prompting, added the formation, VFR, low level and uncontrolled airfield considerations and proposed a mission change that did not reduce the training value. The goal of matching risk to the mission, rather than eliminating it, was stated and applied in the choices made for the route. No IP prompting was required.
texts.4: SP carried the risk assessment into the air, revisiting it when the observed weather, the turbulence or the fatigue level differed from the values assumed in planning, and adjusted the profile accordingly. Deviations from the expected standard on this axis were negligible.

The trend was toward completing the assessment once, on the ground, and then holding the plan unchanged.
